name: Maay
confidence_why: The only first-hand description of Lower Jubba Maay, Paster 2006 (repeated in Comfort and Paster 2009), gives weak root-final stress and no tone from a single consultant, while Saeed 1982 describes the Baydhaba dialect as tonal with high tone mostly on the noun's last syllable, a dialect difference that Paster addresses and that agrees on final placement, so the record rests on one source with no contradiction for its own dialect.
catalog_citation: Paster, Mary. 2006. Aspects of Maay phonology and morphology. Studies in African Linguistics 35(1): 73-120. PDF from journals.flvc.org/sal/article/download/107312/102633
catalog_locator: section 2.2 'Tone or Accent', pp. 76-79 (rule sentence p. 77; verb paradigm p. 78-79; conclusion p. 79)
catalog_quote: However, no such effects of tone or accent are found in LJM. Stress is root-final, but it is not very prominent and is often not distinguishable at all, and the pitch profile of words is predictable based on the number and shape of syllables in the word and the position of the word in the sentence. Saeed (1982: 9) shows that in Central Somali (CS), tone is contrastive on noun roots. According to Saeed, most nouns have final high tone, while some disyllabic roots have initial high tone. As seen in the examples below, both patterns correspond to final stress in LJM. ... In monosyllables, CS contrasts high vs. low tone. There is no such contrast in LJM; all monosyllables are produced with the same kind of word stress. ... Saeed also reports that verbs exhibit characteristic tonal patterns in different morphological contexts in Central Somali (1982: 10). These are absent in LJM. ... Note th…

audit.recode_to: Either (a) split/annotate by dialect: keep 'morphological' (weak root-final stress, no tone) explicitly for Lower Jubba Maay (Paster 2006; Comfort & Paster 2009) and add that Bay-region/Baydhaba Maay ('Central Somali', Saeed 1982 sec. 2.5) has a Somali-type tonal accent -- one H per word; nouns mostly final-H, a lexical set of disyllables initial-H, monosyllables H=masc vs L=fem; verb paradigms with characteristic tone patterns; tonal subject marking -- which under this catalog's conventions (Somali soma1255 coded 'tonal' from Hyman 1981) would be 'tonal'; or (b) if one code must stand for maay1238, reclassify as 'tonal' with a caution that the Lower Jubba dialect has lost the accentual contrasts (Paster 2006: 79). At minimum the the primary-stress rule sentence 'No lexical tone or contrastive stress' must be restricted to LJM and a caution added.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted fragment in the record is verbatim in the Paster 2006 PDF we hold/txt at the stated pages (sec. 2.2, pp. 76-79). (2) Deciding source: a 2006 peer-reviewed phonology/morphology article (48 pp) on Lower Jubba Maay from a single diaspora consultant; the author herself says stress 'is often not distinguishable at all' and explicitly contrasts LJM with Saeed's Central Somali.org): no instrumental or later prosodic study of Maay exists in what I could see; Paster 2018, 2019/2020, Ugas 2015, Addow 2021 are silent (all downloaded and a full-text search for stress/accent); Comfort & Paster 2009 confirms for LJM. sources.citation: Comfort, Jade & Mary Paster. 2009. Notes on Lower Jubba Maay. In M. Matondo, F. McLaughlin & E. Potsdam (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 38th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 204-216. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
sources.quote: 'The Somali dialects that have been described in the literature have contrastive tone or accent ... but no distinctive tone or accent is found in LJM. In this language, stress is root-final.' Same CS-vs-LJM noun, monosyllable, case and verb-paradigm comparisons as Paster 2006 (usbo, boodo, dilmaano final stress; faro, okung final not initial; usu dili ambiguous; root seen stressed throughout the paradigm).
sources.locator: sec. 2.2 'Tone/accent', pp. 205-207; sec. 1 p. 204 (single consultant from Kowan, Lower Jubba)
sources.note: Second published statement of the LJM stress facts (sec. 2.2) with cleaner IPA than the SAL scan; useful as a corroborating citation in the record. downloaded now; confirms.

sources.citation: Saeed, John I. 1982. Central Somali: A grammatical outline. Afroasiatic Linguistics 8(2): 77-119 [issue pp. 1-43]. Malibu: Undena.
sources.quote: 'Central Somali has three phonological tones: a basic high tone versus low tone opposition and a high to low falling tone found over long syllables in some verb forms. Usually only one syllable has high tone, and all polysyllables were found to have one syllable with high tone... This tone opposition could possibly be described in terms of accent or stress. Prominent syllables are higher in pitch, slightly longer ... and louder.' Nouns of 3-4 syllables and most disyllables: H on last syllable (osbá 'salt', boodá 'thigh', dilmaañá 'mosquito'); a small set of disyllables initial H (fárow 'zebra'
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction pp. 2-3 (AAL 8: 78-79: Baydhaba/Bur Hakaba dialect, 'Central Somali (Rahanwin, Af Maymay)', not mutually intelligible with Common or Benaadir Somali); sec. 2.5 Tone pp. 8-11 (AAL 8: 84-86); sec. 5.3 yes-no questions (stress on low-toned question suffix)
sources.note: Primary description of heartland (Bay region/Baydhaba, 'Af Maymay') Maay by a Somali specialist working with multiple speakers; sec. 2.5 documents a Somali-type tonal accent with lexical (noun class, gender on monosyllables) and grammatical (verb paradigm, subject case) contrasts, directly contradicting the record's languoid-level clause 'No lexical tone or contrastive stress', which rests on one Lower Jubba diaspora speaker. downloaded now.
